candidateRows: A belief is rational only when it accords with the reason and evidence available to the believer, whereas faith without sufficient evidence is irrational.
This supplies the operative standard of rationality by which Woodford evaluates theistic belief throughout his opening case and later replies.
Woodford distinguishes rationality from truth, illustrates evidence-sensitive belief with the discarded miasma theory, and contrasts that standard with faith.
Apparently gratuitous suffering makes belief in an all-powerful and all-loving God irrational because such a God could and would prevent evil lacking a greater purpose.
The problem of gratuitous evil is Woodford's principal argument against the rationality of classical theism and structures the later exchange on suffering.
Woodford surveys natural suffering and human atrocity, argues that classical theism must deny every apparent gratuitous evil, and uses an evil-God parity to challenge merely possible theodicies.
Salvation-dependent theism is irrationally contradictory because an all-loving God makes grave consequences depend on disputed propositions while providing widespread religious confusion.
The salvation-confusion argument independently challenges divine love and rational belief, extending the case beyond the evidential problem of suffering.

Woodford argues that traditions disagree about the beliefs required for salvation despite severe possible consequences, then presents this obscurity as incompatible with an all-loving God's supposed plan.
Theism provides a rational basis for trusting human reason, while unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds reliably track truth rather than reproductive success.
This is Edwards's first affirmative argument and directly links God's existence to the reliability of the reasoning faculties used to assess the motion.
Edwards develops an argument from reason and an evolutionary argument against naturalism, contrasting unguided selection for useful behavior with divinely guided minds capable of knowledge.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is vastly more probable on intelligent design than on chance and therefore supports rational belief in God.
Fine-tuning is one of Edwards's three cumulative affirmative pillars for making God's existence more probable than God's nonexistence.
Edwards describes multiple physical parameters as precisely calibrated for life, emphasizes their alleged improbability under chance, and infers an intelligent cause.
Objective moral obligations are best explained by God because denying their objectivity is deeply counterintuitive and impersonal physical reality cannot ground prescriptive moral law.
The moral argument completes Edwards's three-part cumulative case and offers a distinct explanatory route from objective obligation to rational theism.
Edwards invokes widely shared judgments about abuse and discrimination, presents difficulties for both moral anti-realism and atheistic moral realism, and combines morality with reason and design.

The evolutionary argument against naturalism neither establishes theism nor defeats evolved cognition, because atheism does not entail naturalism and selection generally favors broadly accurate beliefs.
This directly contests Edwards's first affirmative pillar by challenging both its characterization of atheism and its inference from evolution to cognitive unreliability.
Edwards's claim that unguided naturalism makes evolved minds unreliable because selection favors survival rather than truth.
Woodford separates atheism from naturalism, notes that refuting an alternative would not itself strongly support theism, and argues that costly false representations are generally selected against.
Theism gives stronger grounds than naturalism for believing that human minds primarily serve truth because intelligence is designed for understanding rather than merely evolutionary success.
This defends the argument from reason against Woodford's evolutionary reply and sharpens the comparative claim that theism better warrants trust in cognition.
Woodford's claim that natural selection generally favors broadly true cognition and therefore does not undermine rational confidence.
Edwards distinguishes occasional overlap between truth and evolutionary utility from a primary orientation toward truth, grounding the latter in designed intelligence and an intelligible world.

Suffering is substantial counterevidence but not a defeater for an all-loving God because Christianity affirms that the world is disordered, includes an afterlife, offers theodicies, and portrays God as sharing human suffering.
This is Edwards's principal direct response to Woodford's central problem-of-evil case and supplies several grounds for retaining rational theism despite suffering.
Woodford's opening contention that apparently gratuitous suffering makes belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God irrational.

Edwards acknowledges evil as the strongest counterevidence, recounts personal suffering, appeals to biblical recognition of disorder, eternal life, established theodicies, and divine solidarity through the cross.

Evolution explains moral reactions to suffering without God, and even successful arguments for a creator cannot establish the Christian or Islamic God when gratuitous evil conflicts with perfect power and love.
Woodford answers Edwards's account of suffering and restates the decisive scope of his evil argument: generic creator evidence cannot establish an omnipotent, perfectly loving deity.
Edwards's claim that atheism cannot affirm that suffering is wrong and that Christian afterlife, theodicy, and divine solidarity answer evil.

Woodford grounds moral intuitions in social evolution, disputes appeals to philosophical and religious authority, and argues that gratuitous evil blocks inference from generic creator arguments to the classical God.
Evolutionary selection can explain moral feelings and persistent moral disagreement under either atheism or theism.
This supplies a naturalistic alternative to divine moral grounding and directly addresses whether atheism can account for moral intuitions.
Edwards's challenge that naturalism cannot affirm that the world is other than it should be.
After Edwards asks whether an atheistic naturalist can coherently judge the world defective, Woodford explains prosocial intuitions and disagreement through evolutionary selection.
Without purpose beyond physical causation, naturalism cannot coherently say that evil makes the world other than it should be.
The challenge links objective moral judgment to purpose and presses a claimed internal limitation of the naturalistic account of evil.
Woodford's evolutionary explanation of moral intuitions and disagreement without divine grounding.
Edwards grants the evolutionary account provisionally but argues that blind physical laws provide no purpose against which atrocities can be judged defective.
Divine-command morality faces a dilemma: goodness is either independent of God or merely the arbitrary dictates of a ruler.
This directly attacks the claimed inference from objective morality to God by arguing that divine command cannot provide a coherent moral foundation.
Edwards's position that objective moral truths require something like God to ground the moral law.
After the moderator restates Edwards's moral argument, Woodford invokes conflicting biblical commands and formulates the two horns of the Euthyphro dilemma.
Modern Western commitments to equal dignity substantially derive from biblical influence, especially the doctrine that every person bears God's image.
The historical claim supports the broader case that biblical theism grounds human value and challenges the use of current moral standards against scripture.
Woodford's use of biblical violence and slavery to argue that divine-command morality is morally arbitrary.
Edwards responds that the standards used to criticize difficult biblical passages were themselves shaped by the Bible's transformative doctrine of universal dignity.
The Euthyphro dilemma is resolved because God commands goodness neither by external conformity nor arbitrary choice, but because God is the good itself.
This is Edwards's direct resolution of the principal objection to divine moral grounding and preserves the claimed connection between objective goodness and God.
Woodford's dilemma that goodness must either exist independently of God or reduce to arbitrary divine commands.
Edwards distinguishes external standards from arbitrary commands and argues that objective goodness is rooted in the character of the creator rather than an abstraction.
Identifying God with goodness only restates the dilemma, since God's nature either aligns with prior goodness or defines goodness arbitrarily.
The reply argues that Edwards's proposed third option does not escape either horn, keeping the central objection to divine moral grounding intact.
Edwards's claim that objective goodness is grounded in God's identity as the good itself.
Woodford characterizes the divine-nature response as postponing rather than answering the issue and reformulates the same independence-versus-definition choice at the level of God's nature.
Recognition of objective goodness is a transcendent intuition whose most adequate source is God rather than an ungrounded abstract concept.
This restates the positive moral argument from experienced objective value to a personal transcendent source and answers the charge of arbitrariness.
Woodford's contention that identifying God with goodness merely repeats rather than resolves the dilemma.
Edwards appeals to deep recognition of real goodness, contrasts a personal divine source with a free-floating abstraction, and says arbitrariness follows only if objective goodness is denied.
Historical evidence for religious figures does not establish miracle claims, which are culturally inherited and unreasonable for an all-loving God to require.
The argument bears directly on the rationality of revealed belief and on whether salvation-relevant assent could justly depend on culturally transmitted miracle claims.
Edwards's qualified affirmation that biblical accounts are real while recognizing different literary genres.
In response to an audience question about biblical truth, Woodford separates likely historical persons from supernatural narratives and compares Christian and Islamic claims.
Human beings exist intentionally because God wanted them, while natural selection may be the guided mechanism through which God brought them about.
This integrates human purpose with evolutionary science, supporting rational theism while avoiding a simple rejection of the dominant natural account of origins.
Answering an audience question about human origins, Edwards denies that people are purposeless accidents, permits guided evolution, and expresses reservations about its total explanatory reach.
Natural selection is not mere randomness, and its strong evidential support now supplies the natural explanation of complexity once monopolized by creation stories.
The response defends evolution against the accident caricature and argues that a well-supported natural mechanism weakens design-based reasons for theistic belief.
Edwards's portrayal of unguided human origins as accidental and his doubts about evolution's complete explanatory capacity.
Woodford distinguishes selection from chance, invokes broad scholarly acceptance, and argues that evolutionary evidence explains biological complexity without requiring traditional creation accounts.
